blocks.text: But if only one or two swallows appear, the proverb of the Greeks is known from Aristotle, Ethics book 1, chapter 6: Μία χελιδὼν ἔαρ οὐ ποιεῖ [mia chelidōn ear ou poiei], One swallow does not make a spring. Among us the swallow's stay is usually six months. Pliny, book 10, chapter 25: Birds differ greatly in their seasons. Some are perennial, like doves; some stay six months, like swallows; some three months, like thrushes and turtledoves. That is, swallows come at the beginning of spring and depart at the end of summer. Pliny on Arcturus, book 18, chapter 31: Let the sign of the rising of that star be observed in the departure of the swallows. Arcturus, moreover, rises in the month of September. Galen: Ἔστι μὲν ὡραιότατον τῆς ἐλάτης τὸ σπέρμα περὶ τὴν ἐπιτολὴν τοῦ Ἀρκτούρου, ὅστις καιρὸς ἐν Ῥώμῃ ὁ καλούμενος μὲν Σεπτέμβριός ἐστι [esti men hōraiotaton tēs elatēs to sperma peri tēn epitolēn tou Arktourou, hostis kairos en Rhōmē ho kaloumenos men Septembrios esti]. It is also around the autumn equinox. Theophrastus on the carob, History of Plants book 4, chapter 2: Ἀνθεῖ περὶ Ἀρκτοῦρον, καὶ ἰσημερίαν [anthei peri Arktouron, kai isēmerian]; or (as Pliny says more explicitly, book 2, chapter 47) Arcturus rises eleven days before the equinox. So when swallows migrate is well enough established, but where they migrate is not likewise. Isidore says in general: (the swallow) flies across the seas and stays there. Anacreon, in the place cited above:
Χειμῶνι δ' εἷς ἄφαντος, Ἢ Νεῖλον, ἢ 'πὶ Μέμφιν. [cheimōni d' heis aphantos, ē Neilon, ē 'pi Memphin.] But in winter you are not seen, [col. 67] Whether you make for the Nile or Memphis.

Herodotus, book 2, chapter 22, on Ethiopia below Egypt: Ἰκτῖνοι δὲ, καὶ χελιδόνες δι' ἔτεος ἐόντες οὐκ ἀπολείπουσι [iktinoi de, kai chelidones di' eteos eontes ouk apoleipousi]; Kites and swallows are there the whole year round, and do not depart in winter. However that may be, among them it is a grave crime to desert the departing flock, if these lines of Martial, book 5, Epigram 68, are true:

When the Attic birds sought their winter retreats in their accustomed manner, one bird stayed behind in the nests: the crime was detected when they returned in springtime, and her own kind tore the deserter to pieces.

But those that remain also face no slight danger from the cold. Pliny, in the passage already cited on the star Arcturus: Let the sign of the rising of that star be observed in the departure of the swallows; for those caught behind perish. Yet it is certain that some remain in sunny places; not all of these die, but they are stripped bare and lose their feathers. Accordingly the Philosopher, History of Animals book 8, chapter 16, after teaching that kites and [II, 613] swallows betake themselves in winter to warmer places when these are not too far away, says: Οἱ δὲ ποῤῥοτέρω ὄντες τῶν τοιούτων οὐκ ἐκτοπίζουσι, ἀλλὰ κρύπτουσιν ἑαυτούς· ἤδη γὰρ ὠμμέναι εἰσὶ πολλαὶ χελιδόνες ἐν ἀγγείοις [hoi de porrhoterō ontes tōn toioutōn ouk ektopizousi, alla kryptousin heautous; ēdē gar ōmmenai eisi pollai chelidones en angeiois] (read ἐν ἄγκεσι [en ankesi], or ἐν ἀγκείαις [en ankeiais]) ἐψιλωμέναι πάμπαν [epsilōmenai pampan]; But the birds that are farther from such places do not migrate from there, but hide themselves: for many swallows have already been seen in valleys, completely featherless. And following him Pliny, book 10, chapter 24: (swallows) go off into neighbouring places, seeking the sunny recesses of the mountains, and have already been found there naked and featherless. To such a swallow Claudian compares the hairless, moth-eaten head of Eutropius, an already worn-out eunuch, in these words, book 1 Against Eutropius:
Or like the winter swallow that, its feathers falling in the icy frosts, dies upon the trunk of a tree.

But when the Prophet says that swallows know the time of their coming or their departure, it need not be understood of all of them without exception. It suffices that it holds for most, so that by this example we may be reminded how rightly Hesiod said:
— — καιρὸς δ᾽ ἐπὶ πᾶσιν ἄριστος [kairos d' epi pasin aristos],
and one of the Seven Sages whom Greece celebrated: Καιρὸν γνῶθι [kairon gnōthi], Know the time. These are the very words of the sacred prophet.
